Setup & first upload

Do this once. Afterwards every lab is: open the example, wire it, upload, open the Serial Monitor.

  1. Install MPLAB XC-DSC v4.00 or newer (the compiler) and MPLAB X (it provides ipecmd, used to program through a PICkit).
  2. Install the Arduino IDE 2.x.
  3. Install the board package with Boards Manager: File → Preferences → Additional boards manager URLs, add
    https://raw.githubusercontent.com/microchipthailand/dspic33ck-nano/main/package_dspicnano_index.json
    then Tools → Board → Boards Manager, search dsPIC33CK Nano and click Install (it also downloads the dsPIC33CK device packs).
    Alternative (for developing the core): copy the folder hardware from arduino\ into your sketchbook folder (File → Preferences → Sketchbook location, usually Documents\Arduino), so you get Documents\Arduino\hardware\dspicnano\dspic33ck\, and restart the IDE. Do not use both at once, or the board appears twice.
  4. Tools → Board → dsPIC33CK Nano (dsPIC33CK256MC005).
    Tools → Clock → 100 MIPS (recommended; Lab 22 requires it).
    Tools → Debugger → your programmer (PICkit 5 on J4).
  5. Plug the board into USB-C (power only — USB-C has no data on this board) and the PICkit into J4 (pin 1 = MCLR, marked on the silkscreen).
  6. For any lab that prints text, plug a 3.3 V USB-serial adapter into J5:
    J5 pinSignalAdapter
    13V3leave open (the board is powered by USB-C)
    2TX = RC10→ adapter RX
    3RX = RC11← adapter TX
    4GNDadapter GND
  7. File → Examples → dsPIC33CK_Nano → Lab01_Blink → Upload. Then Tools → Serial Monitor at 115200 baud for labs that print.
3.3 V only. The dsPIC I/O pins are 3.3 V. Never connect a 5 V signal directly to a pin (Lab 21 and Lab 24 tell you where this matters). The 5V pin (J2-1) is the raw USB voltage — use it only to power modules.
Status: every lab compiles with arduino-cli + XC-DSC at both clock settings (Lab 22 only at 100 MIPS, on purpose) and every J2/J3 pin number quoted here was checked automatically against the PCB netlist. The board has not yet been tested on real hardware, so the “expected output” boxes show what the code is written to print.

Board quick reference

ItemArduino namePinHeader
USER LED (active low)LED_BUILTIN = 34RC13J2-11
USER button (10k pull-up)BUTTON_BUILTIN = 33RC12J2-10
Serial (UART1)SerialTX RC10 / RX RC11J5, J3-4 / J3-3
Serial2 (UART2)Serial2RX RB10 / TX RB11 / DE RB12J2-4 / J2-5 / J2-6
I2CWireSDA RB9 / SCL RB8J3-7 / J3-8
SPISPISCK RC4, MOSI RC5, MISO RC8, SS RC9J3-6, J3-5, J3-14, J3-13
PWMD5 D6 D7 D8RB0 RB1 RB2 RB3J3-21, J3-20, J3-17, J3-16
AnalogA0 A1 A2RA0 RA1 RA2J2-15, J2-16, J2-17
Power–5V, 3V3, GNDJ2-1, J3-1, J2-2 / J3-2

Why LED_ON instead of HIGH? The LED is wired 3V3 → 1k → LED → RC13, so the pin must go LOW to light it. The board package defines LED_ON (=LOW) and LED_OFF (=HIGH) so sketches read naturally.

Why does the button read LOW when pressed? A 10k resistor pulls RC12 up to 3.3 V; the button shorts it to GND.

Timers: Timer1 runs millis(). SCCP1–4 are the PWM channels for D5–D8; tone() borrows SCCP4 (so no PWM on D8 while a tone plays). Lab 13 borrows SCCP3; Labs 14, 16 (frequency check) and 19 (RTOS tick) borrow SCCP2. Labs 15 (DAC), 16 (motor PWM), 22 (WS2812B) and 26 (CAN) need 100 MIPS. The motor-control PWM generators PG1–PG3 (Lab 16) are separate hardware on RB10–RB15.

Learning path: Basics 01–09 = one peripheral at a time with the Arduino API. Advanced 10–19 = register level: pin-change and timer interrupts, interrupt-driven UART, DMA, DAC, motor-control PWM, flash EEPROM, power/reset, a small RTOS. Application 20–27 = complete projects, modules and buses: data logger, GPS, LED strip, OLED, Modbus RS485, LIN, CAN, 10BASE-T1S.

Basics Labs 01–09 · one peripheral at a time, with the Arduino API

01Blink the USER LED

Your first program: prove the tool-chain, the programmer and the board all work.

basicspinModedigitalWritedelay

You need

Just the board + PICkit. Nothing to wire.

Step by step

  1. Open Examples → dsPIC33CK_Nano → Lab01_Blink.
  2. Click Upload. The PICkit programs the chip through J4 (takes a few seconds).
  3. The USER LED flashes: 200 ms on, 800 ms off.
  4. Change the two delay() values and upload again to confirm you are really changing the program.

How the code works

void setup() {
    pinMode(LED_BUILTIN, OUTPUT);          // RC13 becomes an output (TRISC bit 13 = 0)
}
void loop() {                              // loop() runs forever
    digitalWrite(LED_BUILTIN, LED_ON);     // LED_ON = LOW, because the LED is active low
    delay(200);
    digitalWrite(LED_BUILTIN, LED_OFF);
    delay(800);
}

setup() runs once after reset, loop() is called over and over. delay() counts Timer1’s 1 ms interrupts.

Try it

  • Make an SOS pattern: ··· ——— ···
  • Switch Tools → Clock to 4 MIPS: the timing stays the same because delay() is computed from FCY.

02Button toggles the LED (debounce)

Read a digital input and remove contact bounce in software.

basicsdigitalReadmillisdebounceedge detection

You need

Nothing to wire — USER button (RC12) and USER LED (RC13) are on the board.

Step by step

  1. Upload Lab02_ButtonLED.
  2. Press USER once: LED turns on. Press again: off. Each press toggles exactly once.
  3. To see why debouncing matters, set DEBOUNCE_MS to 0 and upload: some presses will now toggle twice (on-off) and look ignored.

How the code works

button pin: HIGH ‾‾‾‾‾|_|‾|_|‾|________________|‾|_|‾‾‾‾‾ (bounces ~1-10 ms) <---- 25 ms ----> stable LOW -> accept the press
  1. Every time the raw reading changes, remember the time (lastChange = millis()).
  2. Only when the reading has not changed for 25 ms is it accepted as the new stableState.
  3. Act only on the falling edge (stable HIGH → stable LOW) so holding the button doesn’t repeat.

Note millis() is used instead of delay(): the loop never stops, which is the pattern every later lab builds on.

Try it

  • Count presses and blink the count back.
  • Long press (> 1 s) = fast blink mode.

03Serial Monitor: print and receive commands

Talk to the PC through the UART header J5.

basicsSerial.beginSerial.printSerial.read

You need

3.3 V USB-serial adapter (CP2102, CH340, FT232 in 3.3 V mode) on J5 as shown in Setup.

Step by step

  1. Wire the adapter: J5-2 (TX) → adapter RX, J5-3 (RX) ← adapter TX, J5-4 → GND.
  2. Upload Lab03_SerialHello.
  3. Tools → Port → the adapter’s COM port, then open the Serial Monitor at 115200.
  4. Press RESET (SW1) to see the greeting. Type 1, 0 or ? and press Enter.

Expected output

Lab 03 - dsPIC33CK Nano says hello!
Send 1 (LED on), 0 (LED off) or ? (status)
tick 0
LED ON
uptime ms = 3521
button    = released
tick 1

How the code works

Serial.available() tells how many received bytes are waiting; Serial.read() takes one. A millis() timer prints a heartbeat every 2 s without blocking command handling — both jobs share one loop.

TX and RX always cross: board TX goes to adapter RX. If you see nothing, swap the two wires first.

04Read a potentiometer with the ADC

Convert a voltage into a number, and the number back into volts.

basicsanalogReadADCSerial Plotter

You need

10 kΩ potentiometer, 3 jumper wires, USB-serial adapter.

Wiring

PotBoard
end 13V3 J3-1
wiper (middle)A0 = RA0 J2-15
end 2GND J3-2

Step by step

  1. Wire the pot, upload Lab04_AnalogRead, open the Serial Monitor.
  2. Turn the knob: raw goes 0 … 1023 and volts 0.000 … 3.300.
  3. Past the middle (raw > 512) the USER LED lights.
  4. Close the Monitor and open Tools → Serial Plotter to see it as a graph.

Expected output

raw=0  volts=0.000
raw=511  volts=1.648
raw=1023  volts=3.300

How the code works

The dsPIC33CK ADC is 12-bit (0–4095). The core shifts the result right by 2 so analogRead() returns the familiar Arduino range 0–1023. Volts = raw × 3.3 / 1023 because full scale is AVDD = 3.3 V.

Lab 14 reads the full 12-bit value straight from the ADC result register.

05PWM: fade an LED

Fake an analog output by switching a pin very fast with a variable duty cycle.

basicsanalogWritePWMmap

You need

One LED, one 330 Ω resistor; the pot from Lab 04 (optional).

Wiring

PartBoard
LED anode (long leg) → 330 ΩD5 = RB0 J3-21
LED cathodeGND
pot wiper (optional)A0 J2-15

Step by step

  1. Upload Lab05_PWMFade. The LED “breathes” up and down.
  2. Hold USER: now the pot sets the brightness directly.

How the code works

duty 25%: _|‾|___|‾|___|‾|___ ~490 Hz, too fast to see -> looks dim duty 75%: _|‾‾‾|_|‾‾‾|_|‾‾‾|_ -> looks bright

analogWrite(5, 0..255) starts SCCP1 in PWM mode on RB0 (routed there by Peripheral Pin Select). map(x, 0, 1023, 0, 255) rescales the ADC reading to the PWM range. Only D5–D8 can do PWM — the USER LED cannot.

06External interrupt on the button

React to an event instantly, without the loop polling for it.

basicsattachInterruptvolatileatomic access

You need

Nothing to wire. USB-serial adapter.

Step by step

  1. Upload Lab06_Interrupt, open the Serial Monitor.
  2. The LED blinks slowly — the loop is “busy”. Press USER: presses: 1, 2, … appear immediately.

How the code works

  1. attachInterrupt(digitalPinToInterrupt(BUTTON_BUILTIN), onButton, FALLING) tells the hardware to call onButton() on every HIGH→LOW edge.
  2. The ISR does the minimum: debounce by time (50 ms) and pressCount++.
  3. pressCount is volatile so the compiler re-reads it from RAM every time.
  4. The loop copies it between noInterrupts() / interrupts() so the ISR can’t change it half-way through a multi-word read.
ISR rules: short, no Serial, no delay(), share data only through volatile variables.

07Play a melody with tone()

Generate audio frequencies and play a tune from arrays.

basicstonearraystimers

You need

Passive piezo buzzer (or 8 Ω speaker with 100 Ω in series).

Wiring

BuzzerBoard
+D9 = RB4 J3-15
−GND

Step by step

  1. Upload Lab07_Tone. The arpeggio C-E-G-C plays once at start-up, LED lit on each note.
  2. Press USER to play it again.

How the code works

melody[] holds frequencies (0 = rest) and duration[] the lengths in ms. tone(pin, f, ms) uses SCCP4 to toggle the pin at f Hz. Waiting 130 % of the note length leaves a short gap so repeated notes are audible.

An active buzzer (the kind with a built-in oscillator) only beeps at one pitch. Use a passive one for melodies.

08I2C bus scanner

Find the address of any I2C module — the first thing to do with a new sensor.

basicsWireI2CACK

You need

Any 3.3 V I2C module (BME280, MPU6050, SSD1306 OLED, 24LC EEPROM…).

Wiring

ModuleBoard
VCC3V3 J3-1
GNDJ3-2
SDARB9 J3-7
SCLRB8 J3-8

Step by step

  1. Wire the module, upload Lab08_I2CScanner, open the Serial Monitor.
  2. Read the address list. Press USER to rescan (e.g. after plugging in another module).

Expected output

Lab 08 - I2C scanner (SDA RB9, SCL RB8)
Scanning I2C bus (0x08..0x77)...
  device found at 0x3C
  device found at 0x76
done, 2 device(s).

How the code works

For each address the master sends a start + address byte. If a device exists it pulls SDA low during the 9th clock (ACK) and endTransmission() returns 0.

Nothing found? Most breakouts have pull-ups; bare chips need 4.7 kΩ from SDA and SCL to 3V3.

09SPI loopback

Test the SPI peripheral with a single jumper wire.

basicsSPISPISettingschip select

You need

One jumper wire.

Wiring

Jumper MOSI RC5 J3-5 ↔ MISO RC8 J3-14.

Step by step

  1. Fit the jumper, upload Lab09_SPILoopback.
  2. LED steady on + errors = 0 = SPI works. Pull the jumper out: LED blinks fast and errors appear.

How the code works

SPI is a shift register: each SPI.transfer(tx) clocks 8 bits out on MOSI and simultaneously 8 bits in on MISO. With MOSI tied to MISO, what goes out comes back. SPISettings(1 MHz, MSBFIRST, MODE0) sets speed, bit order and clock polarity/phase; SS (RC9) is driven by software around the burst.

Next step: replace the jumper with a real device (MCP3008, 25LC EEPROM) and pull SS low around each transaction.

Advanced Labs 10–19 · register level: interrupts, timers, DMA, analog, PWM, flash, power, RTOS

10Pin-change interrupts: Change Notification on many pins + INT1

React to buttons, encoders and fast signals on many pins at once, without polling.

advancedattachInterruptChange NotificationRISING / FALLING / CHANGErotary encoderINT1PPS

You need

A push button, a rotary encoder (or two more buttons), and one jumper. The on-board USER button works with no parts at all.

Wiring

FunctionBoardMode
USER button (on board)RC12FALLING, debounced
button 2 → GNDD21 = RC0 J2-14CHANGE (press and release)
encoder A / B, C → GNDD22 = RC1 J2-20 / D23 = RC2 J2-21CHANGE on both, quadrature
test signal inputD24 = RC3 J3-22RISING, edge counter
jumper for the test signalD9 = RB4 J3-15 → J3-22tone() output
INT1 input (button → GND)D15 = RB10 J2-4external interrupt, falling

Step by step

  1. Upload Lab10_PinChange, open the Serial Monitor. A status line prints on every event.
  2. Press USER: USER=1. Press and release button 2: btn2(change) goes up by 2, because CHANGE fires on both edges.
  3. Turn the encoder: encoder counts up one way and down the other, and the LED toggles with each step. bad steps counts invalid transitions (bounce, or turning too fast).
  4. Jumper J3-15 → J3-22 and send t 1000: the RC3 edge counter climbs 1000 per second and shows the measured period. Try t 20000 to see how fast a CN interrupt can follow.
  5. Ground J2-4 briefly: INT1 counts. That’s the dedicated external interrupt, not CN.

Expected output

Lab 10 - pin-change interrupts: CN on RC12/RC0/RC1/RC2/RC3 + INT1 on RB10. t <Hz>, s, ?
USER=0  btn2(change)=0  encoder=0 (bad steps 0)  INT1=0  RC3 edges=0
USER=1  btn2(change)=2  encoder=-3 (bad steps 0)  INT1=1  RC3 edges=1000 (min period 999 us)

How it works

Change Notification (CN) External interrupt INTx pins EVERY pin of PORTA..PORTD one pin, chosen by PPS (RPINR0.INT1R) edges rising, falling or both, per pin one edge (INTCON2.INT1EP) vectors one per PORT: _CNAInterrupt.._CNDInt. one per INT: _INT1Interrupt which pin? ISR reads CNFx (flag per pin) always the same pin Arduino attachInterrupt() (owned by the core) register level in this lab UNO analogue PCINT0..2 (pin change) INT0 / INT1
  1. CN: CNCONx ON + edge style. CNEN0x/CNEN1x choose rising/falling per pin. CNFx tells the ISR which pin changed. The core’s attachInterrupt() does all this and calls your function, so a sketch must not define _CNxInterrupt itself.
  2. INT1 is set up directly: unlock PPS, map RB10 (RP42) to INT1R, pick the falling edge, priority 5, enable. Its vector is _INT1Interrupt.
  3. Encoder decoding: the two signals step through 00→01→11→10 one way and the reverse the other way. A 16-entry table indexed by old<<2 | new gives +1, −1 or 0 (invalid), so contact bounce cancels itself out.
  4. Debounce: buttons ignore edges closer than 20–40 ms (done in the handler with millis()). The encoder and the test signal must not be debounced, because every edge counts.
Simulator-tested: starts cleanly. CN on PORTC and INT1 are armed (IEC0 = 0x8802 = INT1IE + U1RXIE + T1IE). Edge counting needs real signals, so it’s untested until the board arrives.

11Advanced timers: every hardware time base, with interrupts

Run several independent periodic interrupts at once, pick prescalers, use 16- and 32-bit modes, and measure latency.

advancedTimer1SCCP1–4PG4 as timerprescaler32-bit timerISR prioritieslatency

You need

Optional: an LED + 1 kΩ, a piezo, a scope or logic analyser. It runs with no parts at all (the USER LED blinks from a timer interrupt).

The timers of this chip vs. an Arduino UNO / MEGA

#dsPIC33CK time basetypeused by the core forin this lab
0Timer116-bit timermillis(), delay()only read (reference clock)
1SCCP116/32-bit timer + capture/compareanalogWrite(D5)1000 Hz interrupt, toggles D9
2SCCP216/32-bit timer + capture/compareanalogWrite(D6)100 Hz interrupt, toggles D10
3SCCP316/32-bit timer + capture/compareanalogWrite(D7)10 Hz interrupt, toggles D11 (32-bit mode)
4SCCP416/32-bit timer + capture/compareanalogWrite(D8), tone()left alone (core owns its vector)
5PWM generator PG416-bit PWM time basefreeend-of-cycle interrupt → USER LED
6SCCP1 in 32-bit modeone 32-bit timer–command w: 0.5 Hz without a prescaler

There is no Timer0 or Timer2…Timer9 (T2CON) on this family. The SCCPs do that job. Unlike an AVR, each SCCP can also count in 32 bits.

Wiring (all optional)

SignalBoard
SCCP1 output (500 Hz square wave) → piezo / scopeD9 = RB4 J3-15
SCCP2 output (50 Hz) → scopeD10 = RB5 J3-11
SCCP3 output (5 Hz) → LED + 1 kΩ → GNDD11 = RB6 J3-10

RB5/RB6 are also the PICkit’s PGD/PGC lines (J4). That’s fine while the program runs; unplug the PICkit if it loads them.

Step by step

  1. Upload Lab11_Timers. The USER LED blinks at 1 Hz from PG4’s interrupt, and an LED on D11 blinks at 5 Hz.
  2. Watch the Serial Monitor: once a second it counts each timer’s interrupts against Timer1. You should see exactly 1000 / 100 / 10 per second.
  3. Send 1 2000: SCCP1 goes to 2 kHz (the piezo tone rises). Send 3 1: SCCP3 at 1 Hz, which automatically uses 32-bit mode because 16 bits can’t hold 100 000 000 counts.
  4. Send w: SCCP1 as one 32-bit timer, 2 s period. Send w again to switch back.
  5. Send j: the worst-case interrupt latency of SCCP1 over 1 s, in µs.
  6. Send p: pause/resume all timer interrupts. The pins and the LED freeze while millis() keeps running.

Expected output (from the MPLAB simulator)

Lab 11 - advanced timers: SCCP1/2/3 + PG4 interrupts. 1..3 <Hz>, p, j, ?
# SCCP1 set 1000 Hz -> exact 1000.000 Hz
# SCCP2 set 100 Hz -> exact 100.000 Hz
# SCCP3 set 10 Hz -> exact 10.000 Hz
# over 1000 ms (measured with Timer1 / millis):
#   SCCP1  interrupts/s = 1000.00   set 1000 Hz, pin toggles at 500.00 Hz
#   SCCP2  interrupts/s = 100.00   set 100 Hz, pin toggles at 50.00 Hz
#   SCCP3  interrupts/s = 10.00   set 10 Hz, pin toggles at 5.00 Hz

How it works

SCCPx timer: FCY --[prescaler 1/4/16/64]--> CCPxTMR counts 0..PRL --match--> CCTxIF --> _CCTxInterrupt period: PRL + 1 = FCY / (prescaler x Hz) pick the SMALLEST prescaler that fits 16 bits too slow? T32 = 1: CCPxPRH:PRL is one 32-bit period, no prescaler needed (10 Hz at 100 MIPS = 10 000 000) priorities: SCCP1 = 5 > SCCP2 = 4 > Timer1 = 4 > SCCP3 = 3 > Serial RX = 3 > PG4 = 2 (higher interrupts lower)
  1. Setting up an SCCP as a timer: CCPxCON1L with MOD = 0000 (timer), CLKSEL = FCY, TMRPS = prescaler, then CCPON. CCPxPRL = period − 1. The interrupt vector is _CCTxInterrupt (timer event), not _CCPxInterrupt (capture/compare event).
  2. Exact rates: the sketch prints the frequency the chosen prescaler/period really gives, e.g. 1000.000 Hz. Not every frequency can be hit exactly.
  3. PG4 as a plain timer: PWM generators count PG4PER clocks and can interrupt at the end of every cycle (PG4EVTH.IEVTSEL = 00). With PENH/PENL = 0 the pins stay ordinary GPIO. A counter in the ISR (a “software postscaler”) turns 0.5 ms into 1 Hz.
  4. Latency: the SCCP1 ISR reads its own timer on entry. The count since the period match is the delay. Only a higher-priority ISR, or a noInterrupts()/DISI section, can delay it.
Simulator-tested: SCCP1/2/3 measured exactly 1000 / 100 / 10 interrupts per second. While testing in the simulator I found that a 16-bit SCCP with CCPxPRH = 0 stalls the simulator, so the sketch writes 0xFFFF there, as the core’s own SCCP code does. The simulator doesn’t model the PWM generator, so PG4 (the USER LED blink) shows 0 there; check it on the board.

12UART with interrupts: RX/TX ring buffers on UART3

Write a complete interrupt-driven serial driver on bare registers, and measure why it matters.

advancedUART3RX/TX/error ISRring bufferPPSFIFO

You need

One jumper (test 1), or a second USB-serial adapter (test 2).

Wiring

SignalBoard
U3TXRC0 = D21 J2-14
U3RXRC1 = D22 J2-20

Step by step

  1. Loopback: jumper J2-14 → J2-20. Upload Lab12_UARTInterrupt, open the Serial Monitor. You see u3 rx: Hello from UART3. Type text: it goes out of UART3 and comes back through the RX interrupt.
  2. Send ! for the speed test: blocking Serial.print of 1 kB takes ~90 ms of CPU time. Queuing 256 B into the interrupt driver takes only microseconds, while the wire still needs ~22 ms.
  3. Send # for statistics: bytes, ISR calls, framing/overrun errors, and which TX path is in use.
  4. Second terminal: remove the jumper. Connect adapter 2: its RX → J2-14, its TX → J2-20, GND. Open it at 115200 baud. The two terminals now talk to each other through the board.

Expected output

u3 rx: Hello from UART3
# 1024 B blocking Serial : 89012 us of CPU time
# 256 B  UART3 + IRQ     : 160 us of CPU time, 22300 us on the wire
# rx=37 tx=37 rxISR=5 txISR=4 dropped=0 framing=0 overrun=0 txPolled=0
# TX path: interrupt driven

How the code works

u3Putc() --> txBuf[256] --(TX ISR: "FIFO has room")--> U3TXREG FIFO --> pin RC0 pin RC1 --> RX FIFO --(RX ISR: ">= 1 byte")--> rxBuf[128] --> u3Read() in loop() \--(error ISR)--> framingErr / overrunErr, clear OERR
  1. Setup: power the module (PMD3.U3MD = 0), route the pins through PPS (_RPOUT_U3TX = 27 on RP48, U3RXR = 49), set baud with the fractional generator (BCLKMOD = 1, BRG = FCY/baud), then UARTEN, and only after that UTXEN/URXEN.
  2. RX ISR drains the whole hardware FIFO into a power-of-two ring buffer (& (N-1) instead of %). head is written only by the ISR and tail only by loop(), so no locking is needed.
  3. TX: u3Putc() queues the byte, pushes whatever fits straight into the FIFO, and enables the TX interrupt only if bytes are still waiting. The ISR tops the FIFO up and disables itself when the buffer is empty. Otherwise a level-triggered “FIFO has room” interrupt would fire forever.
  4. Error ISR: framing error = wrong baud or noise. Overrun = the FIFO filled up; clearing OERR restarts the receiver.
  5. Safety net: u3Service() in loop() feeds the FIFO by polling if the TX interrupt never fired. # reports which path did the work.
Simulator-tested: TX, buffering and PPS work. The full greeting arrives on the simulated UART3. But the simulator never raises the UART TX interrupt, so there the polled fallback sends it. On the board, # should report interrupt driven and txPolled=0. If it doesn’t, the UTXISEL encoding needs another look.

13Software serial (a UART built from a timer + 2 pins)

Understand exactly what a UART does by building one in an interrupt routine.

advancedtimer ISRbit timingring bufferregisters

You need

One jumper (test 1); a second USB-serial adapter or another board (test 2).

Wiring

SignalBoard
Soft TXRA3 = D3 J2-18
Soft RXRA4 = D4 J2-19

Step by step

  1. Test 1 — loopback: jumper J2-18 ↔ J2-19. Upload Lab13_SoftwareSerial, open the Serial Monitor. The greeting comes back as soft rx: Hello from…. Type text: it is sent out of the software TX, received by the software RX, and echoed.
  2. Test 2 — bridge: remove the jumper. Second adapter: its RX → J2-18, its TX → J2-19, GND → GND. Open a second terminal on it at 9600. Text typed in either window appears in the other.
  3. Set the second terminal to 4800 baud on purpose: # framing errors: N appears — the receiver detects a missing stop bit.

How the code works

idle ‾‾‾‾|_start_|_b0_|_b1_| ... |_b7_|‾stop‾|‾‾‾‾ 9600 baud: 1 bit = 104 us ticks: | | | | | | timer tick = bit/3 = 34.7 us ^ start seen ^ sample here (1 tick + 3 ticks) = centre of b0, then every 3 ticks
  1. SCCP3 is configured as a plain timer interrupting at 3 × baud (28.8 kHz), at priority 6 so millis() can’t delay it.
  2. TX: the frame (byte << 1) | 0x200 = start 0, 8 data bits LSB first, stop 1. Every 3rd tick shifts out the next bit.
  3. RX: when the idle-high line drops, wait 4 ticks (to the middle of data bit 0), then sample every 3 ticks. If the stop bit is 0 it is a framing error.
  4. Received bytes go into a 64-byte ring buffer (head written by the ISR, tail by the loop — no locking needed).
  5. Pin access in the ISR uses the LAT/PORT register pointers from g_pin_map (much faster than digitalWrite).
Works on PORTA, which has no Peripheral Pin Select — any GPIO will do. But a hardware UART (Lab 21) costs no CPU; use this only when you run out. SCCP3 is D7’s PWM, so no analogWrite(7) in this lab.

14DMA: zero-CPU ADC sampling + memory copy

Let the hardware move the data. A timer triggers the ADC, DMA stores every sample, the CPU only processes full buffers.

advancedDMAhardware triggersping-pong bufferNyquist / aliasing

You need

Potentiometer; optional oscilloscope/logic analyser; one jumper for the aliasing experiment.

Wiring

PartBoard
pot wiper (ends to 3V3/GND)A2 = RA2 (AN9) J2-17
scope probe (optional)D6 = RB1 J3-20 — the 1 kHz sample clock
jumper (aliasing test)D5 = RB0 J3-21 → J2-17 (remove the pot wiper)

Step by step

  1. Upload Lab14_DMA, open the Serial Monitor. The first line says which trigger path worked (see below).
  2. Every 128 ms a line appears with mean voltage, min/max and the AC noise of 128 samples. The LED toggles with each half-buffer.
  3. Turn the pot: mean follows. Leave it still: rms(ac) shows the ADC noise floor in LSB.
  4. Note # CPU idle loop iterations: the CPU is almost entirely free even though it is sampling at 1 kHz.
  5. Send w, then switch to the Serial Plotter: 128 raw samples are drawn.
  6. Send m: DMA channel 1 races a CPU loop and memcpy() copying 256 words 200 times.
  7. Aliasing: remove the pot wiper, jumper J3-21 → J2-17, send p (490 Hz square wave), then w. Instead of a 490 Hz square wave you see a slow ~20 Hz pattern.

Expected output

# trigger path: SCCP2 OC event -> ADC -> DMA (0 CPU per sample)
half 1  mean=1.652 V  min=2045 max=2053  rms(ac)=1.6 LSB  halves=1 overruns=0
half 2  mean=1.652 V  min=2044 max=2052  rms(ac)=1.5 LSB  halves=2 overruns=0
# copy 256 words x200:
#   DMA ch1  ... us total (data OK)

How the data flows

SCCP2 timer ──1 kHz event──▶ ADC converts AN9 ──"AN9 done"──▶ DMA ch0 (PWM on D6, visible) (no CPU) copies ADCBUF9 → adcBuf[i++] │ adcBuf[0..127] ◀── half 1 ──┐ │ adcBuf[128..255] ◀── half 2 ──┴── HALFIF / DONEIF interrupt ◀─────┘ → loop() processes it

How the code works

  1. Sample clock: analogWrite(6,128) lets the core set up SCCP2 (power, pin, PWM mode); the sketch then rewrites its period for exactly 1 kHz.
  2. ADC trigger: ADTRIG2Lbits.TRGSRC9 selects what starts a conversion of AN9. 0x15 = SCCP2 OC event. ADIELbits.IE9 = 1 generates the “done” event, but the CPU interrupt (ADCAN9IE) stays off.
  3. DMA channel 0: source = &ADCBUF9 (fixed), destination = adcBuf (incrementing), count 256, trigger CHSEL = 0x31 (“ADC AN9 conversion complete”), repeated one-shot (one word per trigger) with RELOAD so it wraps forever.
  4. Ping-pong: HALFEN gives an interrupt at half and at full. While the CPU works on one half, DMA fills the other — 128 ms of processing time per half. overruns counts any time the CPU was too slow.
  5. Memory copy: channel 1 in continuous mode, both addresses incrementing, started by software (CHREQ = 1). DMA isn’t necessarily faster than the CPU, but the CPU is free while it runs.
  6. Aliasing: sampling at 1000 Hz can only represent signals below 500 Hz (Nyquist). 490 Hz folds down to |1000 − 2×490| = 20 Hz. Real designs put an analog low-pass filter in front of the ADC.
Trigger-path fallback. Register codes come from Microchip’s MCC device data, but which SCCP event reaches the ADC in PWM mode has not been checked on hardware. setup() therefore tries 0x15 (OC event), then 0x0D (trigger event), and finally falls back to a small SCCP2 interrupt that starts each conversion (DMA still moves the data). The first Serial line tells you which one ran — please note it during bring-up.

15DAC: a true 12-bit analog output + the analog comparator

analogWrite() is only PWM. This chip has a real DAC: DC levels, waveforms, and a hardware voltage-threshold detector.

advanced12-bit DACcomparator CMP1hysteresiswaveformslinearity

You need

One jumper, the potentiometer from Lab 04, optional multimeter/scope. Tools → Clock = 100 MIPS.

Wiring

SignalBoard
DAC outputDACOUT1 = RA3 J2-18
read-back (jumper from J2-18)A2 = RA2 J2-17
comparator input: pot wiperCMP1A = RA0 J2-15

Step by step

  1. Jumper J2-18 → J2-17, upload Lab15_DAC. It starts at 1650 mV and prints the ADC read-back.
  2. Send v500, v2500: measure J2-18 with a meter. It should match within a few tens of mV.
  3. Send l: the linearity table steps the DAC through its range and compares each code with the ADC.
  4. Send s (sine), t (triangle) or c (staircase), then p, and open the Serial Plotter.
  5. Comparator: pot wiper on J2-15, send k2000. Turn the pot: the LED lights above 2.0 V and an interrupt prints comparator edge at every crossing, with no ADC involved.

Expected output

# DC 1650 mV -> read-back on A2: 1648 mV
#  0      0     3     err 3
#  2275   1833  1829  err -4
# comparator threshold = 2000 mV. Turn the pot on J2-15 through it.
# comparator edge #1  pot ABOVE threshold

How the code works

DAC1DATH (12 bit) --> DAC --+--> DACOUT1 pin RA3 Vout = 3.3 V x DATA / 4096 +--> (-) comparator CMP1 --> CMPSTAT bit + CMP1 interrupt pot on RA0 = CMP1A ------> (+) 30 mV hysteresis against chatter
  1. The DAC sits inside comparator module 1. PMD7.CMP1MD = 0 powers it. DACCTRL1L: CLKSEL = FPLLO (the DAC needs the PLL clock, hence 100 MIPS), DACON = master on.
  2. DAC1CONL: DACEN, INSEL = input A (RA0), HYSSEL = 30 mV, IRQM = interrupt on both edges. DAC1DATH = output code.
  3. The comparator answers in nanoseconds, in hardware. In motor control it is the over-current trip that switches the PWM off before software could react.
  4. Waveforms are paced with micros() in loop() (64 samples × 50 Hz). Lab 14 shows the zero-jitter DMA way.
The DAC output is weak (high impedance). Buffer it with an op-amp before driving a load.
Not verified on hardware: this device’s register file shows no separate DAC output-enable bit, so the lab assumes DACEN alone drives RA3. If J2-18 stays at 0 V, the DAC still works internally as the comparator threshold (k). The simulator confirms the registers (DACCTRL1L = 0x80C0, DAC1CONL = 0xE002, DAC1DATH = 2047) but does not model the analog output.

16Advanced PWM: motor-control generators, dead time, 3-phase sine

The “MC” in dsPIC33CK256MC005 stands for Motor Control: four dedicated PWM generators with complementary outputs and hardware dead time.

advancedPG1–PG3complementarydead timecentre-alignedDDS sineinput capture

You need

Logic analyser or scope (best), or 3 LEDs + 1 kΩ, or a 10 kΩ + 100 nF RC filter. Tools → Clock = 100 MIPS.

Pins (fixed PWM pins, no PPS)

GeneratorHigh sideLow sidePhase
PG1PWM1H RB14 J2-8PWM1L RB15 J2-9U (0°)
PG2PWM2H RB12 J2-6PWM2L RB13 J2-7V (120°)
PG3PWM3H RB10 J2-4PWM3L RB11 J2-5W (240°)

Step by step

  1. Set Clock = 100 MIPS, upload Lab16_AdvancedPWM, open the Serial Monitor. The first status line shows the measured PWM frequency (it should read about 20000 Hz).
  2. Scope / logic analyser on J2-8 and J2-9: two complementary 20 kHz signals. Zoom in on an edge: both are LOW for 500 ns. That gap is the dead time. Send d2000 and watch it widen to 2 µs.
  3. LEDs: LED + 1 kΩ from J2-8, J2-6 and J2-4 to GND, then send f1: three LEDs pulse 120° apart, like a rotating magnetic field.
  4. See the sine: J2-8 → 10 kΩ → node → 100 nF → GND, node → A0 (J2-15). Send f5, then a, and open the Serial Plotter: a clean 5 Hz sine. Send m30 for a smaller amplitude.
  5. s = stop (both pins forced LOW by the override logic), g = go.

Expected output

# PER=2500 (expect 20000 Hz)  measured=20000.0 Hz  mod=1.0 Hz depth=80% dead=500 ns  RUNNING  isr/s~20000

How the code works

centre-aligned counter: /\/\/\/\ f_pwm = f_clk / (2 x PER) = 100 MHz / 5000 = 20 kHz PWM1H ___|‾‾‾‾‾‾|________|‾‾‾‾‾‾|___ PWM1L ‾‾|_|‾‾‾‾‾‾‾‾|_|‾‾‾‾‾‾‾‾|_|‾ <- complementary, with dead time (both LOW) at every edge duty(t) = PER/2 + PER/2 x depth x sin(phase + 0 / 120 / 240 deg)
  1. Clock: PCLKCON.MCLKSEL = 00 selects FCY as the PWM master clock. PGxCONL: CLKSEL = master clock, MODSEL = 100 centre-aligned, ON.
  2. Outputs: PGxIOCONH: PENH + PENL (the PWM module owns both pins), PMOD = 00 complementary. PGxDTH/DTL = dead time in clock ticks (50 = 500 ns).
  3. Synchronised: PG2 and PG3 have SOCS = 0001, so they start each cycle together with PG1 and the three phases stay locked. PG1 is switched on last.
  4. Sine by DDS: PG1’s end-of-cycle interrupt fires at 20 kHz. A 32-bit phase accumulator advances by f × 2³² / 20000, and its top 8 bits index a 256-entry sine table. Phases V and W read the table 85 and 171 entries further on (120° and 240°).
  5. Glitch-free: new duty values go into PGxDC. UPDREQ makes the hardware load them at the next cycle start, never in the middle of a pulse.
  6. Safety: PGxIOCONL.OVRENH/OVRENL force both pins to the override level (LOW). That’s the same mechanism a hardware fault input uses.
  7. Self-check: SCCP2 in 32-bit input-capture mode, wired to RB14 through PPS, timestamps 8 rising edges and computes the real frequency.
These are logic-level signals. Never connect them directly to MOSFETs or a motor. A real inverter needs gate drivers and a fault input. Also, RB10–RB12 are the Serial2/RS485 pins of Labs 21 and 24.
Not verified yet: the MPLAB simulator does not model the PWM generator. It confirms the registers are set up (PG1CONL = 0x800C, PER = 2500, DC = 1250), but there is no output or interrupt. Whether the PWM really counts at FCY will only be known on the board, which is why the sketch measures and prints the frequency. If it shows 10 kHz or 40 kHz, the clock is FCY/2 or 2×FCY: scale PCLK_HZ to match.

17EEPROM emulation in Flash

This chip has no data EEPROM. Store settings in program Flash, so they survive power-off.

advancedNVM controllerpage erasedouble-word writewear levellingCRC

You need

Nothing to wire. USB-serial adapter on J5.

Step by step

  1. Upload Lab17_EEPROM, open the Serial Monitor. The first start prints no valid record - first start and bootCount=1.
  2. Press RESET a few times: bootCount counts up. Unplug USB-C and plug it back in: it keeps counting.
  3. Send b100: the LED blinks fast. Power-cycle: still fast. The setting was saved to Flash.
  4. Send v1234 to save a number, then d to dump the records. Each save appends a new record: slot 0, 1, 2…
  5. Send f (factory reset) then RESET: back to the defaults.

Expected output

Lab 17 - EEPROM emulation in Flash.  ? b<ms> v<num> d f
# boot counted and saved
bootCount=3  blinkMs=500  userValue=0
  page 0 @0x2A000  slot 3/102  seq 3  writes this run 1

How the code works

Flash 0x2A000 page 0 [rec seq0][rec seq1][rec seq2][ FFFF erased ... ] <- active, append here Flash 0x2A800 page 1 [ FFFF erased ................................... ] <- spare record = 5 double words: MAGIC | seq | bootCount | blinkMs | userValue | 0 0 0 | CRC | ~CRC page full (102 records) -> erase page 1, write newest record there, page 1 becomes active
  1. Flash rules: Flash bits can only go 1→0 when written; only an erase sets them back to 1, and only a whole page at a time. The smallest write is a double word (2 instruction words), and each word can be written once per erase.
  2. Unlock: every erase or write sets NVMADR and NVMCON (NVMOP 0011 = page erase, 0001 = double word), loads the data latches through TBLPAG = 0xFA, then __builtin_write_NVM() writes 0x55/0xAA to NVMKEY and sets WR. Interrupts are masked (DISI) during the unlock. These are the same routines as the board’s bootloader.
  3. Log structure: a save never overwrites anything. It appends a record. At startup, eeLoad() scans both pages and takes the valid record with the highest sequence number. One erase therefore covers 102 saves, about 2 million saves in total at 10 000 erase cycles per page.
  4. CRC + inverted copy: a power cut in the middle of a write leaves a half-written record. Its CRC fails, so it is ignored and the previous good record wins.
  5. Where it lives: uint16_t eeArea[2048] __attribute__((space(prog), address(0x2A000), noload)). noload means the linker reserves the space but puts nothing in the .hex. That matters because the Serial bootloader checks a CRC of the application before every start, so data that changes must lie outside that range. A second noload block reserves the gap above 0x2B000, so the linker can’t place code up there, out of reach of short calls.
Settings survive RESET and power-off, but any new upload (PICkit or Serial bootloader) erases them, because both erase the whole application area.
Simulator-tested: in the MPLAB X simulator bootCount went 1 → 2 → 3 across three resets, and the hex file contains nothing from 0x2A000 up, in either memory layout.

18Power saving & reset sources: Doze, Idle, Sleep, POR, BOR, WDT

Find out why the chip started, and cut its power with the three low-power modes.

advancedRCONPOR / BORwatchdogDozeIdleSleepwake-up

You need

Nothing to wire. Optional: a USB power meter in the USB-C cable to see the current drop.

Step by step

  1. Upload Lab18_PowerReset, open the Serial Monitor. The first lines show RCON and the reset reason.
  2. Make each reset happen: press RESET → EXTR MCLR pin. Send r → SOFTWARE reset. Send w → WATCHDOG reset. Unplug USB-C for 2 s → POWER-ON. The “starts since power-on” counter survives every reset except a power-off.
  3. Send 1 (RUN): note the loop count and the current.
  4. Send 2 (DOZE 1:128): the LED still blinks at exactly 2 Hz, but the loop count is about 128× smaller and the current drops. Peripherals keep full speed; only the CPU is slowed.
  5. Send 3 (IDLE): the CPU stops between Timer1 ticks. It reports woke 3000 times in 3 s, one per 1 ms tick.
  6. Send 4 (SLEEP): everything stops (LED off, UART silent). Press USER to wake it. millis() advanced only a few ms while you waited, because Timer1 was stopped too.

Expected output (from the MPLAB simulator)

# RCON = 0x83 : [POR power-on] [BOR brown-out] [EXTR MCLR pin]
# reset reason: POWER-ON (POR+BOR are both set at power-up)
# executing RESET instruction...
# RCON = 0x40 : [SWR software]
# reset reason: SOFTWARE reset (RESET instruction)
# IDLE done, woke 3000 times (= 1 per Timer1 tick)
# RCON = 0x10 : [WDTO watchdog]
# reset reason: WATCHDOG reset - the program stopped feeding the WDT

How the code works

CPU Timer1/millis UART ADC/PWM wakes on RUN full yes yes yes - DOZE 1:128 /128 yes (full) yes yes - (ROI=1: any interrupt ends Doze) IDLE off yes yes yes any enabled interrupt SLEEP off NO NO NO pin change (CN), INTx, WDT
  1. Reset reason: RCON collects a flag for every reset cause. The sketch reads it first in setup(), then clears it, so the next reset reports only its own cause. At power-up POR and BOR are both set.
  2. POR / BOR: the power-on reset holds the chip in reset until VDD is valid. The brown-out reset does the same whenever VDD sags below the BOR trip point, so the CPU never runs on a voltage too low to be reliable. On this family the BOR is always on.
  3. Watchdog: config bit FWDTEN = ON_SW lets software switch it on (WDTCONL.ON). If the program then stops calling ClrWdt(), the WDT resets the chip. That’s how a product recovers from a hung loop. The period comes from config bit RWDTPS; this board uses the shortest one.
  4. Doze: CLKDIV.DOZE = ratio, DOZEN = 1. Idle: Idle() = PWRSAV #1. Sleep: Sleep() = PWRSAV #0. The USER button wakes it because attachInterrupt() uses change notification, which needs no clock.
  5. Persistent RAM: __attribute__((persistent)) tells the C start-up code not to zero a variable, so it survives a reset (but not power-off).
Simulator-tested: power-on, software reset and watchdog reset all produced the right RCON flags, and Idle woke exactly once per ms. Sleep and the current figures need the real board.

19RTOS: a preemptive real-time kernel from scratch

See what FreeRTOS does inside, by building a tiny version: tasks with their own stacks, preemption, priorities, sleep, a semaphore.

advancedcontext switchschedulerprioritiessemaphoreinline assembly

You need

Nothing to wire. Serial Monitor on J5.

Step by step

  1. Upload Lab19_RTOS, open the Serial Monitor. The LED blinks (task blink), and every second report prints a table of all the tasks.
  2. Watch load=: about 20–30 % with the worker in light mode.
  3. Press USER: [button] press #1 handled at tick … appears at once. The button task has the highest priority and preempts everything.
  4. Send w: the worker goes HEAVY (never sleeps). Load jumps to 100 %, idle stops gaining time, worker and report share the CPU round-robin, and the LED still blinks on time (higher priority). That is real-time scheduling.
  5. Look at stack used/512: every task has its own stack, and the table shows how much of it was ever used.

Expected output (from the simulator, shortened)

t=1029 ms  switches=139  primes=837  load=68%  worker=light
   idle   prio 0 READY    ran 480 ms  stack 72/512
   blink  prio 2 SLEEPING ran 0 ms  stack 90/512
   button prio 3 BLOCKED  ran 0 ms  stack 90/512
   worker prio 1 SLEEPING ran 200 ms  stack 102/512
   report prio 1 READY    ran 738 ms  stack 168/512

(report uses a lot of CPU in the simulator because Serial.print waits for the UART. On the board at 115200 baud expect a few %.)

How a context switch works

task A running -- 1 ms tick ISR (SCCP2, IPL2): wake sleepers, pick best READY task, pend switch \- switch ISR (CRC vector, IPL1 = lowest, like PendSV on ARM) push W0-W14, RCOUNT, TBLPAG, DSRPAG, DSWPAG, CORCON, MODCON, ACCA, ACCB, DO regs tasks[A].sp = W15 SPLIM = 0xFFFF; W15 = tasks[B].sp; SPLIM = B's limit pop all of B's registers RETFIE --> task B continues where it was interrupted
  1. TCB: each task has a saved stack pointer, a stack limit, a priority, a state (READY / SLEEPING / BLOCKED), a wake-up tick and a run-time counter.
  2. Scheduler: picks the highest-priority READY task. Among equal priorities it takes the next one after the current task (round-robin). The idle task is always READY.
  3. Switch in assembly: it runs at the lowest interrupt priority, so it never splits another ISR. It raises its own CPU priority to 7 while it works, and switches SPLIM together with W15, so a stack overflow traps instead of corrupting the next task.
  4. New task: rtosCreate() builds a fake “interrupted” frame (PC = task function, SR = IPL0, 32 zeroed registers) so the first RETFIE “returns” into the task.
  5. rtosDelay(ms): marks the task SLEEPING until kTicks + ms and switches away. semTake() marks it BLOCKED. semGiveFromISR() (called by the button’s attachInterrupt) makes it READY and requests a switch.
  6. Serial lock: two tasks printing at once would mix characters. lockSerial() waits with rtosDelay(1), not just a yield. A high-priority task that only yielded would be picked again immediately, the low-priority owner would never finish, and the system would deadlock (priority inversion).
Resources: SCCP2 (D6’s PWM) is the kernel tick and the unused CRC interrupt is the switch vector. Simulator-tested: preemption, round-robin, sleeping, blocking, stack use and the load figure all behave as described. Timer1/millis() keep running underneath.
This is a teaching kernel. For a product use a proven RTOS, e.g. the official FreeRTOS dsPIC33 port, which does the same things with many more safety checks.

Second hardware UART, text-protocol parsing, checksums, and real-world data.

Wiring

GNDJ3-2

Step by step

Expected output

utc,date,lat,lon,fix,sats,hdop,alt_m,speed_kmh
083015.00,111126,13.756331,100.501765,1,7,1.2,12.4,0.3

How the code works

  1. Line assembly — feedGps() collects characters from Serial2 until CR/LF. A $ always restarts the line, so a corrupted sentence can’t poison the next.
  2. Checksum — XOR of every character between $ and * must equal the two hex digits after *. Bad lines are counted and dropped.
  3. Fields — splitFields() replaces commas with string terminators in place (no copying, and empty fields stay as empty strings).
  4. RMC gives time, valid flag, lat/lon, speed (knots × 1.852 = km/h), date. GGA gives fix quality, satellites, HDOP, altitude.
  5. Coordinates arrive as ddmm.mmmm: degrees = dd + mm.mmmm/60, negative for S/W.
$GNRMC,083015.00,A,1345.37986,N,10030.10590,E,0.162,,111126,,,A*6F
        time     ok  lat  ddmm.mmmm     lon dddmm.mmmm  knots date    checksum

22WS2812B addressable RGB LEDs via SPI

Generate a strict 800 kHz one-wire protocol with a peripheral instead of fragile bit-banging.

applicationSPI as waveform generatorbit encodingtiming

You need

WS2812B strip/ring/stick (8 LEDs by default), 330 Ω resistor, 470–1000 µF capacitor across strip power. Tools → Clock = 100 MIPS (the sketch refuses to compile at 4 MIPS).

Wiring

StripBoard
DIN→ 330 Ω → MOSI RC5 = D26 J3-5
5V5V J2-1 (≤ 8 LEDs from USB)
GNDGND J2-2 (common ground is mandatory)

Step by step

  1. Wire the strip (capacitor across 5V/GND at the strip), set Clock = 100 MIPS, upload Lab22_WS2812B.
  2. A rainbow runs. Press USER for: running dot → breathing blue → R/G/B test → rainbow.
  3. In the R/G/B test, LED 0 must be red, LED 1 green, LED 2 blue. If red/green are swapped your strip is RGB-order, not GRB.
  4. Change NUM_LEDS / BRIGHTNESS for your strip (keep brightness low on USB power: 60 mA per LED at full white).

How the code works

WS2812B bit = 1.25 us SPI at 3.333 MHz: 1 SPI bit = 300 ns, 4 SPI bits = 1.2 us LED '0' = 0.40 high + 0.85 low -> SPI 1000 (300 ns high) LED '1' = 0.80 high + 0.45 low -> SPI 1110 (900 ns high) 1 colour byte = 8 LED bits = 32 SPI bits = 4 SPI bytes; PAIR[] = {0x88,0x8E,0xE8,0xEE}
  1. setPixel() stores colour scaled by brightness in G, R, B wire order.
  2. show() pre-encodes the whole frame into SPI bytes first, so transmission is back-to-back.
  3. Interrupts are off during transmission — a millis() tick mid-stream would stretch a bit. Every encoded byte ends in a 0, so the small gap between SPI bytes only lengthens a LOW phase, which the LED tolerates.
  4. 80 µs of LOW afterwards = “latch”: the LEDs show the new colours.
A 5 V WS2812B wants VIH ≥ 3.5 V; 3.3 V data usually works with short wires. If it flickers: 74AHCT125 level shifter, or power the strip at ~4.5 V.

23OLED display: SSD1306 graphics driver from scratch

Initialise the controller, keep a frame buffer, draw pixels, lines and text with your own font, and stream it over I2C.

applicationSSD1306I2Cframe bufferBresenhambitmap font

You need

0.96″ SSD1306 OLED, 128×64, I2C (4 pins). Optional: the potentiometer from Lab 04.

Wiring

OLEDBoard
GNDJ3-2
VCC3V3 J3-1
SCLRB8 J3-8
SDARB9 J3-7
pot wiperA0 RA0 J2-15

Step by step

The dashboard screen (rendered on the PC from the sketch’s own drawing code)

How the code works

SSD1306 RAM = 8 pages x 128 columns, 1 byte = 8 vertical pixels (bit0 = top) pixel(x,y) -> fb[(y/8)*128 + x] bit (y%8) whole screen = 1024 bytes I2C: [addr 0x3C] [0x00 = commands follow] cmd cmd ... [addr 0x3C] [0x40 = data follows] 16 bytes of fb x 64 transactions
  1. Init sequence (from the SSD1306 datasheet): display off, clock, multiplex = 63, offset 0, charge pump ON (0x8D 0x14, needed at 3.3 V), horizontal addressing, segment remap + COM scan direction (so the image isn’t mirrored), contrast, display on.
  2. Frame buffer: every drawing call only changes RAM. oledShow() sets the window to the full screen (0x21 columns, 0x22 pages) and streams all 1024 bytes.
  3. Chunks: this Wire library buffers 32 bytes per transmission, so each transaction carries 1 control byte + 16 data bytes.
  4. Graphics: line() is Bresenham’s algorithm (integers only). rect() builds on it, and text uses a 5×7 font table (96 printable ASCII characters × 5 column bytes) with integer scaling.
  5. No floating point in the display path: the voltage is formatted from millivolts with integer maths, which is faster and smaller than printf.
The drawing code was checked by running the same algorithms on the PC: the screen above is the real 128×64 frame buffer. That caught the layout and the font, not the I2C link, which needs a real display.

24Modbus RTU over RS485 (master + slave)

A real industrial fieldbus: half-duplex physical layer, binary frames, CRC-16, timeouts, exceptions.

applicationRS485Modbus RTUCRC-16protocol state

You need

Two boards + two RS485 transceiver modules (SP3485 / THVD1500 3.3 V preferred), twisted pair. Or one board + a USB-RS485 dongle + a PC Modbus tool (Modbus Poll, QModMaster, mbpoll).

Wiring (each board)

RS485 moduleBoard
RORB10 = D15 J2-4 (Serial2 RX)
DIRB11 = D16 J2-5 (Serial2 TX)
DE + /RE tiedRB12 = D17 J2-6 (HIGH = transmit)
VCC / GND3V3 / GND
A, BA↔A, B↔B to the other board; 120 Ω across A-B at both ends of a long cable; join GNDs
A 5 V MAX485 module drives RO at 5 V — divide it down (e.g. 1 k / 2 k) before RB10.

Step by step

  1. Upload Lab24_ModbusRS485 to both boards.
  2. Board A: just reset → SLAVE id 1 (LED blinks slowly = waiting).
  3. Board B: hold USER while pressing RESET, release → MASTER. Open its Serial Monitor.
  4. The master prints the slave’s registers twice a second. Turn the pot on the slave’s A0 — A0= changes; press the slave’s USER — btn=1.
  5. Press the master’s USER: it writes register 2 and the slave’s LED toggles.
  6. Unplug the A wire: read failed: timeout. That is how a fieldbus master detects a dead node.

Expected output (master)

Lab 24 - Modbus RTU MASTER (polling slave 1)
slave1: A0=512 btn=0 led=0 up=14s req=27  (ok 27 / fail 0)
write LED=1 ok
slave1: A0=515 btn=0 led=1 up=15s req=29  (ok 28 / fail 0)

Slave register map

ModbusRegMeaningAccess
400010analogRead(A0)R
400021USER button 1/0R
400032LED 0/1R/W
400043uptime sR
400054request counterR

How the code works

request  (fn 03): [01][03][00 00][00 05][CRC lo][CRC hi]     id, function, start reg, quantity
response        : [01][03][0A][r0 hi][r0 lo] ... [r4 lo][CRC lo][CRC hi]
exception       : [01][83][02][CRC]     fn | 0x80, code 01 bad function / 02 bad address / 03 bad value
  1. Framing by silence: a frame ends after 3.5 character times without a byte (4.0 ms at 9600). receiveFrame() uses micros() to measure that gap.
  2. CRC-16/MODBUS: init 0xFFFF, polynomial 0xA001 (reflected), sent low byte first. Wrong CRC or another address → the slave stays silent (as the spec requires).
  3. Half-duplex: Serial2 raises DE on the first byte; flush() waits for the last stop bit (TRMT) before dropping DE — releasing it earlier would cut off the CRC.
  4. The master uses a 200 ms response timeout and counts ok/fail.

25LIN bus: master and slave at 19200 baud

The low-cost single-wire car body bus: break, sync, protected ID, data and checksum, built byte by byte on UART2.

applicationLIN 2.xbreak / syncPID parityclassic & enhanced checksumschedule table

You need

Test 1: one jumper. Test 2: two boards, two LIN transceivers (MCP2003B, TJA1021, TLE7259), a 12 V supply.

Wiring

SignalBoardTransceiver
UART2 TXRB11 = D16 J2-5TXD
UART2 RXRB10 = D15 J2-4RXD (open drain, internal pull-up on)
Test 1: just jumper J2-5 → J2-4. Test 2: EN/CS → 3V3, VBAT → 12 V, LIN wires joined, GND common, master: 1 kΩ + diode LIN→VBAT.

Step by step

  1. One board: jumper J2-5 → J2-4, upload Lab25_LIN (USER released = MASTER). Every frame is read back from the “bus”. ? shows bitErrors=0, so everything sent arrived unchanged. “no answer to 0x20” is expected, because there’s no slave.
  2. Two boards: board B started with USER held = SLAVE. The master now prints slave 0x20: A0=… btn=… alive=… every 0.5 s.
  3. Press USER on the master: frame 0x10 carries the LED command and the slave’s LED toggles.
  4. Send c on only one board: classic vs enhanced checksum mismatch → badChecksum rises. Send e to fix it.

Expected output (master, two boards)

Lab 25 - LIN 19200 baud, MASTER (schedule 0x10 / 0x20)
# PID(0x10)=0x50  PID(0x20)=0x20
slave 0x20: A0=512 btn=0 alive=17
# LED command -> 1

How a LIN frame looks

|<-- BREAK >= 13 bits low -->|del| SYNC 0x55 | PID | D0 | D1 | ... | Dn | CHECKSUM | \______________ header (always sent by the MASTER) _____/\_____ response (publisher) _____/ PID = ID(6 bits) + P0 = ID0^ID1^ID2^ID4 + P1 = !(ID1^ID3^ID4^ID5) 0x10 -> 0x50, 0x3C -> 0x3C checksum = ~(sum with carry wrap) classic: data only enhanced (LIN 2.x): PID + data
  1. Break: U2MODE.BRKOVR = 1 forces TX low for 13 bit times (677 µs). A slave sees it as a 0x00 byte with a framing error, which is how it finds the start of a frame.
  2. Sync 0x55 = alternating bits, so a slave with an imprecise RC oscillator can measure the master’s bit rate (auto-baud).
  3. Echo check: on a single-wire bus every node hears itself. txEcho() compares each echoed byte; a difference means a bit error or collision.
  4. Schedule table: the master alternates 0x10 (it publishes) and 0x20 (the slave publishes) every 50 ms. In LIN only the master starts frames.
The PID and checksum functions were checked against known values (ID 0x3C → PID 0x3C; classic checksum of 4A 55 93 E5 = E6). The UART also has a hardware LIN mode (MOD = 1100) that automates break/sync/checksum. This lab builds the frame by hand so every field is visible. Hardware test pending.

26CAN FD controller: frames, filters, loopback, a real bus

The car/industrial bus: bit timing, a transmit queue, a receive FIFO with an acceptance filter, error counters.

applicationCAN 2.0B / CAN FD500 kbit/sbit timingmessage RAMfiltersTEC/REC

You need

Step 1: nothing (internal loopback). Step 2: a CAN transceiver per board (MCP2562FD, SN65HVD230, TJA1051) and a second node (another board or a USB-CAN adapter). Clock = 100 MIPS.

Wiring (step 2)

SignalBoardTransceiver
CAN TXRC6 = D27 J2-22TXD
CAN RXRC7 = D28 J3-18RXD
power5V J2-1 (+ 3V3 J3-1 to VIO on MCP2562), GNDVDD / VIO, STBY → GND
busCANH–CANH, CANL–CANL, 120 Ω at both ends

Step by step

  1. Upload Lab26_CAN. It starts in internal loopback: every 500 ms it sends ID 0x123 and receives it back, and the LED toggles.
  2. Send ?: mode, TX/RX counters and the error counters TEC/REC, “error-active” = healthy.
  3. Wire two boards with transceivers, send n on both: each now prints the other’s frames.
  4. From a USB-CAN tool, send ID 0x120 with byte0 = 1 / 0: the board’s LED follows (remote control).
  5. Unplug CANH: no ACK → TEC climbs → error-passive → bus-off. That’s CAN’s fault confinement at work.

Expected output

# mode=INTERNAL LOOPBACK  tx=1 (queue full 0)  rx=0  TEC=0 REC=0  error-active
rx id=0x123 dlc=8 : 00 01 FF 00 CA FE 00 00
rx id=0x123 dlc=8 : 01 01 FE 00 CA FE 00 00

How the code works

CAN clock: FVCO 400 MHz / 4 / 5 = 20 MHz 1 bit = 40 tq of 50 ns = 2 us = 500 kbit/s |sync|<------------ TSEG1 = 31 tq ------------>|<-- TSEG2 = 8 tq -->| sample point 80 % message RAM (in normal data RAM, C1FIFOBA): [TXQ: 4 objects][FIFO1 RX: 8 objects] object = T0 (11-bit ID) | T1 (DLC, IDE, RTR, BRS, FDF) | data 0..3 | data 4..7
  1. Clock: CANCLKCON: CANCLKSEL = FVCO/4, CANCLKDIV = ÷5 gives 20 MHz. Bit timing (C1NBTCFG): BRP 0, TSEG1 30, TSEG2 7, SJW 7.
  2. Modes (C1CONH.REQOP, read back from OPMOD): 4 = configuration (required to change timing/FIFOs), 2 = internal loopback, 6 = normal CAN 2.0.
  3. TX: the CPU writes the next free object (address from C1TXQUA), then sets UINC + TXREQ. RX: filter 0 + mask 0x700 accepts IDs 0x100–0x1FF into FIFO1. The interrupt copies each object out and sets UINC to free it.
  4. Pins: PPS, CAN1TX code 21 on RC6, CAN1RXR = RP55 (RC7).
Not verified on hardware: the MPLAB simulator doesn’t run the CAN module (the mode request stays pending), so this lab is compile-verified only. One detail is open: whether CxFIFOUA holds an absolute address or an offset. objPtr() accepts both. If ? still says “configuration”, the mode change did not complete; check CANCLKCON and, for normal mode, the transceiver’s RXD.

2710BASE-T1S single-pair Ethernet (LAN8651 MAC-PHY over SPI)

Put the board on automotive/industrial single-pair Ethernet: 10 Mbit/s, one twisted pair, multidrop, collision-free with PLCA.

applicationIEEE 802.3cg10BASE-T1SPLCAOPEN Alliance TC6SPIEthernet frames

You need

Two LAN8651 boards, e.g. MikroE Two-Wire ETH Click, on two Nano boards. Or one, plus a 10BASE-T1S USB adapter (e.g. Microchip EVB-LAN8670-USB) and Wireshark on a PC.

Wiring

LAN8651 clickBoard
SCK / SDI(MOSI) / SDO(MISO)RC4 J3-6 / RC5 J3-5 / RC8 J3-14
CSRC9 J3-13
IRQ (active low)RB7 = D12 J3-9
RSTRD8 = D36 J3-12
3V3 / GNDJ3-1 / J3-2
T1S pair: N–N, P–P between the clicks; 100 Ω termination at both ends of the pair.

Step by step

  1. Upload Lab27_10BaseT1S to board A (USER released = PLCA node 0, the coordinator) and to board B with USER held at reset (node 1).
  2. Each prints OA_ID / OA_PHYID. A non-zero PHY ID means SPI and the MAC-PHY are working.
  3. Every second each node broadcasts an Ethernet frame (EtherType 0x88B5) with the text dsPIC33CK Nano node N count C, and prints the other node’s frames.
  4. With a USB adapter + Wireshark you see the same frames on a PC, as real Ethernet.

Expected output

Lab 27 - 10BASE-T1S via LAN8651 (OPEN Alliance TC6 over SPI)
# OA_ID=0x..  OA_PHYID=0x........   (non-zero = MAC-PHY answering; exact values per LAN8651 datasheet)
# PLCA node 0 of 8 (coordinator)
rx 64 B from 02:00:00:00:00:01 type 0x88B5  "dsPIC33CK Nano node 1 count 7"
# tx 8  rx 7  credits 31  chunk errors 0

How the code works

10BASE-T1S multidrop: node0 ──┬── node1 ──┬── node2 ... (one twisted pair) PLCA: node 0 sends a BEACON, then each node ID gets a transmit opportunity in turn -> no collisions TC6 control: [hdr: DNC=0 WNR MMS ADDR LEN P] [data] [echo] register read/write TC6 data: [hdr: DNC=1 DV SV EV EBO P][64 bytes] <-> [64 bytes][footer: RCA TXC DV SV EV ...]
  1. Why a MAC-PHY: the dsPIC has no Ethernet MAC. The LAN8651 contains MAC + PHY and talks over plain SPI, so any MCU with SPI can join an Ethernet network.
  2. Control transactions: a 32-bit header (memory map selector MMS, address, length, odd parity) reads or writes registers. The MAC-PHY echoes the header one word later.
  3. Data transactions: Ethernet frames move in 64-byte chunks. SV marks the first, EV + EBO the last. The footer of every chunk reports how many RX chunks are waiting (RCA) and how many TX buffers are free (TXC).
  4. PLCA (Physical Layer Collision Avoidance): node IDs 0…N-1 take turns, giving a guaranteed, deterministic latency on a shared wire.
Not verified on hardware: written from the OPEN Alliance TC6 specification and the LAN865x register map as I know it. Check the register addresses (OA_PHYID, PLCA_CTRL0/1 in MMS 4, MAC NCR) and Microchip’s recommended LAN8651 initialisation writes (their lan865x driver / application note) before relying on it. The sketch prints each step so you can see where it stops.

Troubleshooting

SymptomCheck
Upload fails / PICkit can’t find the deviceUSB-C power plugged in? J4 pin 1 (MCLR) aligned with the PICkit arrow? Tools → Debugger matches your tool? MPLAB X installed (for ipecmd)?
Compile error mentioning xc-dsc-g++Install XC-DSC v4.00 or newer.
Nothing in the Serial MonitorPort = the adapter’s COM port, 115200 baud, TX/RX crossed (J5-2 → adapter RX), adapter in 3.3 V mode, common GND. Press RESET to see start-up text.
Garbage charactersWrong baud rate in the Monitor, or the Clock menu changed without re-uploading.
LED works backwardsUse LED_ON/LED_OFF, not HIGH/LOW — the LED is active low.
analogRead always 0 or 1023Wire on the right header pin (A0 = J2-15, not J3-15)? Pot ends on 3V3 and GND?
PWM / tone stops unexpectedlytone() and D8 PWM share SCCP4; Lab 13 uses SCCP3 (D7); Labs 14, 16 and 19 use SCCP2 (D6).
I2C scanner finds nothingPull-ups present? SDA/SCL swapped? Module is 3.3 V?
Lab 21 “no GPS data”GPS TX → J2-4, 9600 baud, GPS powered (its own LED blinks once it has a fix).
Lab 22 flickers / wrong coloursClock = 100 MIPS, common GND, 330 Ω in series, big capacitor; check colour order with effect 3.
Lab 24 timeoutsA/B swapped? DE+/RE on J2-6? Both boards 9600? Slave started without USER held?
Lab 14 “trigger path: NONE”The DMA/ADC setup needs register-level debugging — report the line printed and check DMACNT0 in the debugger.
Lab 17 settings lostExpected after any upload (the upload erases the app area). They only survive RESET / power-off.
Lab 16 measured frequency is not 20 kHzThe PWM clock is not FCY on your silicon: scale PCLK_HZ (e.g. FCY/2). “no edges on RB14” = PWM not running: check Clock = 100 MIPS.
Lab 12 says “POLLED fallback”The UART3 TX interrupt did not fire. Data still flows; report it so the UTXISEL setting can be corrected.
Lab 19 freezes / resetsA task stack overflowed (SPLIM trap): raise STACK_WORDS; check the “stack” column.
Lab 23 “no OLED at 0x3C”Run Lab 08; try OLED_ADDR 0x3D; SDA/SCL swapped? Blank but found: wrong OLED_H (32 vs 64).
Lab 18 never wakes from SleepPress USER (RC12). Sleep stops the UART too, so the PC sees nothing until wake-up. RESET always works.
Lab 15 J2-18 reads 0 VJumper to J2-17 for the read-back. If the pin stays at 0 V, DACOUT1 may need an output-enable this lab doesn’t set; the comparator (k) still works.
Lab 26 stays in “configuration” / bus-offClock = 100 MIPS? Normal mode needs a second node to ACK, a transceiver on RC6/RC7, 120 Ω at both ends. Use l (loopback) to test alone.
Lab 25 bitErrors risingJumper/transceiver on J2-5/J2-4? Same checksum type (c/e) on both nodes? 12 V on the transceivers’ VBAT?
Lab 27 OA_PHYID = 0 or FFFFFFFFSPI wiring (MISO on RC8), CS on RC9, RST on RD8 high, 3V3 to the click. Then check the register map against Microchip’s LAN865x driver.
